claims.text: Thermomechanical treatment, such as optimized annealing, enhances oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Thermomechanical treatment enhances oxidation resistance by refining the alloy microstructure.
The proposed microstructural refinement reduces grain-boundary density.
Thermomechanical treatment can optimize precipitate formation or distribution.
Reduced grain-boundary density and optimized precipitates promote formation of a more uniform and protective oxide scale.
As-processed multiprincipal-element alloys typically possess heterogeneous microstructures after casting or initial processing.
Grain boundaries and dislocation networks are fast diffusion pathways relevant to oxidation.
Reducing fast diffusion pathways and optimizing precipitate distribution jointly promote a continuous protective oxide scale.
Grain boundaries act as rapid diffusion paths for oxygen in the proposed alloy systems.
A microstructure with fewer grain boundaries facilitates development of a more coherent and adherent oxide scale.
A coherent and adherent oxide scale slows oxidation kinetics.
Slower oxidation kinetics preserve material integrity during high-temperature exposure.
Treated alloys will develop thinner oxide scales than untreated controls under the same oxidation conditions.
Treated alloys will develop more uniform oxide scales than untreated controls.
Treated alloys will exhibit less oxidation-associated weight gain than untreated controls.
Treated alloys will retain better mechanical properties, including creep or degradation resistance, than untreated controls.
The proposed behavior should hold for multiprincipal-element alloys of similar compositional complexity under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
Large composition changes or environments not dominated by oxidation may fall outside the hypothesis's applicability.

contradictions.description: The treatment is repeatedly described as refining the grain structure while also reducing grain-boundary density and producing fewer grain boundaries. Grain refinement ordinarily denotes smaller grains and therefore greater grain-boundary area per unit volume; the intended change may instead be grain coarsening or reduction of defect density. This unresolved terminology makes the intervention-to-mediator link internally inconsistent.
